data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back into Popper's system because any rational basis for preferring one conjecture over another inevitably relies on an implicit assumption that the future will resemble the past (the uniformity of nature), which Popper explicitly rejected.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can demonstrate a non-inductive rationale for preference that does not rely on future success expectations.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'rationality' of the decision is purely aesthetic or sociological rather than epistemic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the assumption of nature's uniformity is not required for the specific act of choosing the best-tested theory.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Even if labeled a 'decision,' the act of preferring a well-tested theory over an untested one implies a belief that the testing process is relevant to future performance. If there is no inductive link, the preference is arbitrary. Since Popper insists the preference is rational and not arbitrary, he must be smuggling in an inductive principle: that surviving tests makes a theory more likely to succeed in the future, contradicting his denial that corroboration equals probability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
